title: The Khalsa shall rule
hookLine: a couplet after Ardas speaks of the Khalsa ruling; Sikhs understand it in several ways, from justice to spiritual sovereignty

lines: AFTER THE ARDAS, A SUNG COUPLET.
cards: The Ardas is over. The congregation is still standing, hands folded. Then the whole room sings a short couplet together, loud and steady.
It opens with three words in Punjabi: raj karega Khalsa. The Khalsa shall rule. For a visitor hearing it the first time, it can land with a jolt.
Rule over whom? Rule how? Fair questions, and Sikhs themselves answer them in more than one way.

teach.b: Where it comes from: the couplet isn't in the Guru Granth Sahib. Tradition attributes it to Guru Gobind Singh, and it's recorded in one of the old codes of Sikh conduct.
Its next lines say, in paraphrase, that none will stay defiant, that those who wandered in misery will come together, and that those who take shelter will be safe.
Tradition says it was sung through the hunted century by people with a price on their heads.
That's the first way Sikhs hear it: a promise of sovereignty, said aloud when it looked impossible, and remembered later when Sikh chiefs did hold the land. The second way is justice.
Guru Arjan, in the Guru Granth Sahib, describes a rule where, in paraphrase, by the merciful one's command no one pushes another around, no one hurts another, and everyone lives at ease.
He calls it halemi raj, a gentle rule. Some readers hear the couplet through that line: a rule where nobody is crushed. The third way turns inward.
Khalsa can mean the pure, those who belong directly to the Guru.

teach.h: THE FIRST KINGDOM IS THE SELF.
teach.b: In this reading, the first kingdom to rule is the self: anger, greed, ego, fear. Someone who can't rule their own temper isn't ready to rule anything else. These readings don't cancel each other.
Sikhs hold them side by side, and different gurdwaras and teachers lean different ways. The third is the one anyone can try today.

how: In gurdwaras the congregation often sings the couplet beginning raj karega Khalsa after the Ardas, standing, and Sikh teachers explain it as sovereignty, as just and gentle rule, and as mastery of the self.

o: a gentle rule where no one hurts another
the Khalsa's victory over its enemies
a king's law enforced by the sword

games.q: three ways to hear one line — tap the pairs.

s: the couplet is a line from the Guru Granth Sahib
it isn't in the Guru Granth Sahib. tradition attributes it to Guru Gobind Singh, in an old code of conduct.
Sikhs read the couplet in only one way
they hear sovereignty, justice and rule over the self, and hold them side by side.
Guru Arjan describes a rule where no one hurts another
he calls it halemi raj, a gentle rule.

games.q: you're a hunted rider. the band has almost nothing. after the Ardas everyone sings that the Khalsa shall rule. what's the point of singing it now?
o: to say aloud, while it looks impossible, what they trust is coming.
games.why: Sikhs remember the couplet being sung through the hunted century, a promise said aloud when it looked furthest away.

practice: Ask one plain question: what in me tends to take over, temper in traffic, the phone at midnight, worry that runs the morning?
Name just one, then picture the next time it rises and, for one breath, choosing what happens next, not crushing it, just being the one in charge. If you pray, rest in Waheguru as you breathe.

wordCard.voice: halemi raj, the gentle rule Guru Arjan describes, where no one pushes another around and everyone lives at ease. Sikhs hear it in the couplet sung after the Ardas, alongside sovereignty and ruling one's own self. Today's word.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: the Khalsa shall rule, the opening of the couplet sung after the Ardas.

carryVoice: Your line: rule yourself first. Three readings, held side by side. That's eight hundred eighty-one days.
